newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to keep Nazi-hunting centre open.
newsitem.headline: Germany to keep Nazi-hunting centre open.

text.p: Germany will keep its investigation centre for Nazi war crimes open for as long as there are cases to be prosecuted, a state justice minister said on Friday.

Ulrich Goll of Baden-Wuerttemberg said justice ministers from the 16 federal states had decided at a Bonn meeting to maintain the centre in Ludwigsburg, near Stuttgart. The decision would be formally announced later on Friday.
The future of the centre, which is funded by the states, was in doubt because the number of Nazi trials has dwindled and its long-time director Albert Stein died this summer.

But the ministers decided the centre should stay in operation and preparations made to turn it into a public research centre rather than turn its files over to any other institution, Goll told journalists.
"This clears the way for a secure future for the centre," he said, adding that its investigations could last another 10 years.

Founded in 1958, the centre gathers and sorts all available documents about Nazi crimes in World War Two to establish the whereabouts of the culprits. Last year it cost 2.2 million marks ($1.46 million) to run.
Veteran Nazi-hunter Simon Wiesenthal appealed to the justice ministers earlier this week to keep the centre open.
"I would urge those responsible not to close the centre and to think about the consequences of doing so... Closure would be seen abroad as negative," Wiesenthal said.
"No institution has done as much, or as seriously, for German honour as the centre in Ludwigsburg... Whoever has been concerned with Nazi crimes and criminals for decades must also finish the job."
